candidate_decisions.reason: The focus and 17:14 support the guided/lost course, self-accounting, nontransferable burden, and messenger threshold. The bearer/burden terms retain the core load and liability branches, while 17:2 and 17:22 activate the shared-root refuge branch only as a qualified contextual resonance about the limits of substitute reliance.

The indexed focus guidance and self forms connect to the journey, induced seeing, and book-made guidance in 17:1-2. Those exact context roots and coordinates support the attributed reading that personal benefit does not make guidance self-originated.

The traced 17:3, 17:6, and 17:7 occurrences show collective carriage, material aid, and reflexive benefit; the focus burden and self forms return that support to the distinct question of who bears moral liability. The 17:3 link remains contextual and qualified.

The focus dispatch and messenger coordinates align with the earlier dispatch in 17:5 and the command-response-destruction sequence in 17:16. The procedural interval is retained as an attributed contextual inference, including its stated alternative.

The focus self and guidance forms meet the supplied 17:9 guidance, 17:11 haste and mistaken harm-seeking, and 17:12 differentiation. The trace supports fallibility as a contextual reading while leaving open whether 17:11 concerns only impatient requests.

The exact 17:13-14 account sequence attaches, opens, and has each person read an account before 17:15 states the burden rule. The focus load and self forms provide the return contact for this identity-bound reading.

The focus course and self forms are followed by contrasted desires and efforts in 17:18-19, provision for both in 17:20, and differentiated degrees in 17:21. Every traced root and index matches the supplied context occurrences; the material-only alternative remains explicit.

The focus helper/load branch contacts the prohibition on assigning one's affair to a trustee in 17:2 and the warning against installing another deity in 17:22. The proxy reading survives as an analogy about accountable agency, not a ban on ordinary support.

The focus burden forms map to the supplied prepared-speech branch, while the 17:13-14 written, opened, self-read account supplies an independent counter-record. The split-root/outlier status is preserved as exploratory and not treated as the lexical translation of the burden word.

findings.title: A Personal Account and a Burden That Stays
findings.claim: The focus places guidance or loss with the acting self, then gives that personal consequence a load-bearing form: another bearer cannot assume it. The immediately preceding attached and self-read account makes this responsibility inspectable; 17:2 and 17:22 frame substitute reliance against that rule, while the messenger clause places a notice threshold before punishment.
findings.mechanism: The paired guidance and straying forms meet the bearer, burden, and other-burden terms; 17:13-14 has already attached a record to each person and made that person read it. The warnings in 17:2 and 17:22 activate the shared-root refuge branch contextually: a substitute protector cannot remove the self's burden. In the focus, hatta links sending a messenger to the limit on punishment. Together these contacts make the burden personal without making the person self-sufficient or uninformed.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see one movement from chosen direction, through an account that returns to its reader, to a burden no other bearer can take; the earlier warnings add a qualified contrast with seeking substitute refuge, not a ban on ordinary help, and a messenger condition on punishment.
findings.containment: The load remains the ordinary carrier of the primary claim. The lost-way branch colors straying without claiming a literal missing object; the sufficiency image in 17:14 is a nominated contextual branch. The refuge branch is only a pericope-level contextual resonance from 17:2 and 17:22; it does not make every trustee, helper, or source of aid a forbidden refuge. The sentence sets a messenger threshold but does not supply the later response sequence.

epistemic.reason: The trusted channel evidence directly anchors 17:14-15; lost-object, sufficiency, and refuge facets are contextual branch applications. The refuge reading depends on the earlier trustee warning and later abandonment warning, so it remains bounded rather than lexicalizing the focus's burden word as refuge.

findings.title: A Furnished Route, a Personal Yield
findings.claim: The focus says guidance benefits the self; 17:1-2 lets that benefit be read as received along a route and book already furnished from beyond the self.
findings.mechanism: The focus guidance verbs and self-reference are the carriers. The enacted night journey and showing in 17:1, followed by the book made guidance in 17:2, independently supply a route, signs, and articulation. Their contact changes personal benefit from an apparent self-originated achievement into the yield of a course the self takes up.
findings.reader_payoff: Personal responsibility need not mean that the person invents the guidance by which the course is found.
findings.containment: The route and book context adds provision without making the guided person passive or displacing the self as beneficiary. The live alternative is that the journey is analogy only and the focus concerns consequence, not guidance's source.

epistemic.reason: The focus/context coordinates and roots match the packet, but the causal inference from furnished guidance to the focus's source of direction remains an attributed HFT reading.

findings.title: Support Without Substituting for the Bearer
findings.claim: The focus denies transfer of the accountable load, not every kind of carrying or aid: 17:3 carries a people, 17:6 extends resources, and 17:7 says good and harm return to the actors themselves.
findings.mechanism: The focus's load-bearing words are activated by three distinct contextual acts: collective carriage, material support, and reflexive moral return. Their contact marks a boundary between assistance that can reach a person and liability that remains attached to that person's course.
findings.reader_payoff: The negation no longer sounds like a ban on help; it names what help cannot do, which is take another person's accountable place.
findings.containment: The 17:3 carriage is only an analogy to the focus and a connection note explicitly resists treating it as a direct burden parallel. The contextual reading distinguishes bodily or material support from moral transfer without claiming the verses explicitly classify every form of help.

epistemic.reason: The traced roots and coordinates agree with supplied context occurrences. The help-versus-liability distinction remains an attributed macro inference, especially for 17:3.

branch_activations.independent_trigger: Collective carriage in 17:3 and aid in 17:6 independently show that carrying and support can occur.
branch_activations.activation: Contextual carriage meets the focus's no-other-bearer phrase and distinguishes physical support from taking its load.
branch_activations.resulting_reading: The focus can deny liability transfer without denying that someone may help or carry another.
branch_activations.boundary: The distinction is contextual and does not define all forms of burden.

findings.title: From Dispatch to Response and Verdict
findings.claim: The messenger threshold can be heard as the opening of an accountable response interval: the later town sequence in 17:16 places address and a response before a due verdict and destruction.
findings.mechanism: The focus pairs punishment with sending a messenger. Earlier 17:5 uses the same dispatch root for forceful agents; later 17:16 orders a town, records its transgression, makes the word due, and destroys it. Those distinct scenes contact the focus's messenger threshold and make notice part of a larger address-response-verdict movement.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can perceive a procedural shape around the word until, rather than hearing it as an unexplained delay after a messenger merely appears.
findings.containment: The procedural arrow is the HFT author's inference. The 17:16 command is not identified as a messenger, and the focus may state temporal precedence without expanding a legal rule. These contextual distinctions remain visible.

epistemic.reason: All listed context coordinates and roots match the packet's occurrences, but the claim that the sequence supplies a response interval is explicitly an attributed inference.

findings.title: A Responsible Self Can Misread Its Own Good
findings.claim: The focus still returns guidance and error to the self, while 17:9-12 shows why that self cannot be assumed to discern its good unaided: guidance points toward what is upright, haste can call for harm as if for good, and the signs are differentiated.
findings.mechanism: The focus self-reference and guidance/straying pair are the carriers. Quranic guidance and uprightness in 17:9, the mistaken harm-request shaped like a good request in 17:11, and detailed differentiation in 17:12 independently contact the choosing self. Their contact changes personal responsibility from presumed clear-sighted choice to accountable choice that can need communicated distinction.
findings.reader_payoff: The self can remain responsible without being portrayed as an infallible judge of its own direction.

findings.title: Personal Courses Within Shared Provision
findings.claim: The focus locates the result of guidance or straying in the self, and 17:18-21 develops two desired courses without making either person the source of the whole field in which effort takes effect: both receive provision, and their outcomes unfold by degrees.
findings.mechanism: The focus guidance and self forms carry personal course and yield. In 17:18-19, desire is paired with hastening or effort and with different horizons; 17:20 extends provision to both groups without a barrier; 17:21 adds unequal degrees. This sequence contacts the focus's self-directed result and changes it from a closed merit economy into personal striving within shared provision.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can hold responsibility and dependence together: a course belongs to its chooser even when its opportunities and realization are not self-produced.
findings.containment: The material gift in 17:20 may concern worldly provision only and need not modify how the focus's guidance works. The contextual inference remains attributed; it neither erases personal effort nor turns outcomes into a flat two-way verdict.

epistemic.reason: The complete pericope sequence supports desire, effort, provision, and gradation; the nested-agency synthesis is explicitly an attributed HFT inference, with a live material-only reading.

findings.title: A Proxy Cannot Assume the Account
findings.claim: The focus's burden-bearing helper image is bounded by the pericope's warnings against handing one's affair to a trustee or setting another deity beside God: guidance and aid may arrive from beyond the self, but an installed proxy cannot take over the self's accountable agency.
findings.mechanism: The focus helper/load carrier meets the trustee prohibition in 17:2 and the closing warning in 17:22. The latter ends in blame and abandonment rather than successful substitution. This contact changes the no-other-bearer line from a rule only about one human carrying another's penalty into a contextual resistance to outsourcing one's accountable course.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can distinguish receiving help from appointing a substitute to choose or answer in one's place.
findings.containment: The focus's helper image and the two prohibitions make an analogy, not an explicit equation. The 17:2 and 17:22 warnings may concern reliance or worship without directly explaining burden transfer; ordinary human aid is not prohibited here.

epistemic.reason: The focus branch is independently registered and each traced context coordinate agrees with the supplied surface, but the move from trusteeship and worship to outsourced accountability remains an attributed analogy.

findings.title: A Record That Resists Rhetorical Reassignment
findings.claim: At an exploratory split-root branch level, the focus load-carrier can also resonate with preparing and shaping speech. The immediately preceding written, opened, self-read account then makes the no-transfer rule resistant to rhetorical reassignment as well as to another person physically bearing the load.

The ordered writing in 17:13 and reading/accounting in 17:14 independently provide a counter-record. Their contact changes the rule into a resistance to narrating liability onto another bearer, while the written and self-read account remains the check.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see how personal accountability withstands a changed telling of who owns the burden.
findings.containment: This is exploratory, uses the packet's non-dominant split-root mapping, and must not be rendered as the lexical translation of the focus load word. The ordinary physical and moral load remains intact; the account imagery may signal inescapability without specifying rhetoric.

epistemic.reason: The exact mapped focus occurrence and 17:13-14 context are supplied, but the speech-preparation branch is an explicitly exploratory outlier with legacy-unbound attribution.

findings.title: A Shared Request, an Individual Account
findings.claim: Read with the added Fātiḥa verses, 17:15's self-specific result does not imply an isolated or self-sufficient seeker: the focus's guidance and help-bearing language meets a plural request for help and a straight path, while its own burden remains with each bearer.
findings.mechanism: The focus self, guidance/straying pair, and load are the carriers. Fātiḥa 1:5 asks for help in a plural voice; 1:6 asks to be guided to the straight path; 1:7 names the strayed as a contrary path. These distinct triggers contact the focus's own-self and burden relations, changing personal accountability from isolation into an individual course pursued within shared dependence.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see shared seeking and personal responsibility together: help and guidance may be asked for collectively without transferring one person's account to another.
findings.containment: This is an external overlay from 1:5-7, not a claim that 17:15 itself is plural or a prayer. The added verses do not say that one person carries another's moral burden, and the focus's own-self result remains intact.

epistemic.reason: The external ayat and focus words directly supply the contact, while the reading of plural seeking as a frame for individual accountability is an interpretive overlay beyond the literal syntax.
